name: Focal nodular hyperplasia
aliases: focal nodular hyperplasia of the liver

reference.source: Sherlock's Diseases of the Liver and Biliary System / EASL benign liver tumour guidance
clinicalPearls: The second most common benign liver tumour, usually an incidental finding in women of reproductive age and typically solitary
Regarded as a hyperplastic response to a pre-existing arterial malformation rather than a true neoplasm, with essentially no malignant potential and very low bleeding risk
The characteristic feature is a central stellate scar containing a large feeding artery, best appreciated on cross-sectional imaging
Contrast studies show intense, uniform arterial-phase enhancement with a spoke-wheel vascular pattern and delayed enhancement of the central scar
Hepatobiliary contrast-enhanced MRI is particularly useful, as FNH characteristically retains contrast in the hepatobiliary phase, helping distinguish it from adenoma
Unlike hepatocellular adenoma, it is not strongly driven by oestrogen and generally does not require oral-contraceptive cessation or resection
Asymptomatic, radiologically typical lesions are managed conservatively with reassurance and, if desired, interval imaging
reference.pathophysiology: Focal nodular hyperplasia is a polyclonal, non-neoplastic proliferation believed to arise from a localised hyperplastic hepatocyte response to an anomalous dystrophic artery. The aberrant arterial supply produces a central fibrous scar containing thick-walled vessels that radiate outward, dividing the lesion into nodules separated by fibrous septa containing malformed ductules. Because the architecture is a reactive rather than clonal neoplastic process, the lesion carries negligible risk of haemorrhage or malignant transformation, in contrast to hepatocellular adenoma.
additionalInvestigations: Multiphase contrast-enhanced MRI or CT to demonstrate arterial enhancement and central scar
Hepatobiliary contrast agent MRI to show retention in the hepatobiliary phase
Contrast-enhanced ultrasound demonstrating a spoke-wheel arterial pattern
Alpha-fetoprotein and clinical context to help exclude malignancy
Percutaneous biopsy reserved for lesions with atypical imaging features
redFlags: Atypical imaging features raising concern for fibrolamellar or hepatocellular carcinoma
Rapid growth or new symptoms in a previously stable lesion
Diagnostic uncertainty in a patient with chronic liver disease or known malignancy
Abnormal liver biochemistry or rising tumour markers
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is excellent; most lesions remain stable or regress, complications are rare, and there is no meaningful risk of malignant transformation, so intervention is seldom needed.
pitfalls: Confusing FNH with hepatocellular adenoma and mismanaging bleeding and malignancy risk
Overlooking fibrolamellar carcinoma, which can also feature a central scar
Performing unnecessary resection of a radiologically classic, asymptomatic lesion
Attributing all central-scar lesions to FNH without adequate imaging characterisation
references: Sherlock's Diseases of the Liver and Biliary System
EASL Clinical Practice Guidelines on the management of benign liver tumours
